_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 9 Connected Devices. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: who joins the network, working together, wired and wireless, whether the network is there, sharing, and what you keep to yourself. The devices, the examples and the apps are the lesson's own. The one drawing lifted whole from the kit is ART.figure(tablet), drawn plain and large in the offline test, because the lesson's own offline step runs on a tablet; everything else is drawn here, because Computing keeps its home network, its signal bars and its cables inside closures a film cannot reach. ART.scene(internet) is not used: at states 2 and 3 its caption is wider than its own viewBox and clips, and states 0 and 1 are two computers on a wire, which is not what this lesson teaches.
title: Connected Devices
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Identify a range of devices that can connect to a network, including to the internet.
Know that two devices working together can achieve things that neither device can achieve on its own.
Know that there are wired and wireless networks.
Know how to recognise when a network is and is not available.
Know that network connected devices share information with each other and that there are risks associated with this.

beats.say: Phones, printers, speakers, consoles, TVs and watches all join the network.
Joined together, two devices do what neither can alone.
A network is not only computers. Lots of devices can join one.
A laptop browses the web. A tablet plays videos, games and messages.
A phone joins at home. A printer prints for every device in the house.
A smart speaker fetches music. A games console plays with a friend.
A smart TV streams a film. A smart watch shows messages on your wrist.
A wooden chair cannot join, because it has no computer inside.
The others all join through the router, and reach the internet.
A phone takes a photo, but a phone cannot print it.
A printer prints, but a printer cannot take a photo.
Join them both to the network. Now the photo can travel.
The phone sends it. The printer prints it. Neither could do both.
A phone holds a song, and a speaker plays it loud. Two devices, one job.
A wired network joins its devices with cables.
An office has a cable from every computer to the wall.
A school computer room has cables under the desks.
A wireless network joins them through the air, with wi-fi.
Tablets at home and phones on a train are wireless. Many places have both.
Your device tells you whether the network is there.
Bars on the phone mean it is available. So does a green light.
No bars, aeroplane mode or a dark router mean it is not.
A page that spins and never loads usually means no network.
Then the things that need other devices stop, and the rest carry on.
Devices on a network share information with each other.
What you send is seen by every device it goes to.
A message to the class group goes to the whole class. Think before you send.
Something posted for anyone to see can be seen by strangers.
Your full name, your address, your school: that is personal information.
Share it on a network, and you cannot take it back.
A password is for you and a grown-up only. Keep it private.
Some files are malware, made to do harm. Never open one from a stranger.
Lots of devices join a network, and through it, the internet.
Two together do what neither can alone. Cables are wired, wi-fi is wireless.
Bars and lights say it is there. Think who will see what you share.
